introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: one and three quarter hours.**

Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
> "If the average cost curve stops falling and starts to rise when the firm is producing only a small fraction of the total industry sales, there is no cost advantage in being a giant and many competitors enter the industry. This situation sounds like perfect competition, but it is not if the firms are producing a differentiated product. In this case, the result is monopolistic competition. Because each firm is selling a somewhat different product, each has some control over price; **if it raises its price slightly, it won't lose all its customers.** Thus it does not face the perfect competitor's perfectly horizontal demand curve. Instead, its demand curve slopes downward to the right. But because of the existence of many competitors, its control over price is not great."

*Source: Economics by Wonnacott 2nd Edition p.557*

*(In the printed paper the sentence in bold, "if it raises its price slightly, it won't lose all its customers", is underlined.)*

figures.legende: Firm in long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition: downward-sloping AR = D tangent to the ATC curve at the output where MC = MR, price P* equal to ATC, with excess capacity (model answer to Q5(a)(i); illustrative, no real data).

Firm in long-run equilibrium under perfect competition: horizontal P = MR = AR = D line touching the minimum of ATC where MC cuts ATC, at output Q* (model answer to Q5(a)(ii); illustrative, no real data).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Sketch the long-run equilibrium price and output diagrams of:

(i) the monopolistic competitor. (4 marks)

(ii) the perfect competitor. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Monopolistic competitor (firm diagram).** Draw price, costs and revenue (FCFA) on the vertical axis and output on the horizontal axis. Draw:

- a **downward-sloping demand curve** $AR = D$ (fairly elastic, because there are many close substitutes) with the **marginal revenue** curve $MR$ below it;
- a U-shaped **average total cost** curve $ATC$ and an upward-sloping **marginal cost** curve $MC$ cutting $ATC$ at its lowest point.

Long-run equilibrium: the firm produces where $MC = MR$, output $Q^*$, and charges the price $P^*$ read on the demand curve. Entry of new firms (while supernormal profits exist) shifts the demand curve of each existing firm to the left until **$AR$ is just tangent to $ATC$ at $Q^*$**. So $P^* = ATC$: the firm earns only **normal profit**. The tangency lies on the falling part of $ATC$, to the left of its minimum: the firm has **excess capacity**, and $P^* > MC$.

![fig-1](gce-al-economics-2023-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_1.png)

**(ii) Perfect competitor (firm diagram).** Same axes. Draw:

- a **horizontal line** $P = MR = AR = D$ at the market price (the firm is a price taker);
- the U-shaped $ATC$ curve and the rising $MC$ curve cutting $ATC$ at its minimum.

Long-run equilibrium: free entry and exit remove any supernormal profit or loss, so the price line **touches $ATC$ at its lowest point**, and the firm produces $Q^*$ where $P = MR = MC = \text{minimum } ATC$. The firm earns only **normal profit**, produces at the lowest cost (productive efficiency) and $P = MC$ (allocative efficiency). (A second diagram for the industry, with market demand and supply meeting at $P^*$, may be added to show where the price comes from.)

![fig-2](gce-al-economics-2023-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_2.png)

questions.enonce_markdown: Give three differences between a perfect competitor and a monopolistic competitor. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
| | Perfect competitor | Monopolistic competitor |
|---|---|---|
| **Product** | **Homogeneous**: all firms sell identical products. | **Differentiated** (brand, quality, design, packaging, location), so products are close but not perfect substitutes. |
| **Demand curve and price** | **Perfectly elastic (horizontal)** demand: the firm is a **price taker** and has no control over price. | **Downward-sloping, relatively elastic** demand: the firm has **some control over price** (a price maker within limits). |
| **Selling costs / competition** | No advertising, as the firm can sell all it wants at the market price: only price competition. | **Non-price competition**: advertising, branding and product development are important. |
| **Long-run efficiency** | Produces at the **minimum point of $ATC$**, and $P = MC$ (productive and allocative efficiency). | Produces on the **falling part of $ATC$** with **excess capacity**, and $P > MC$. |
| **Knowledge** | Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of prices. | Knowledge is imperfect: buyers do not know all the differences between brands. |

Any three of these rows, each with the contrast explained, earn the 6 marks (2 marks for each difference). Both structures have many firms and free entry and exit, and only normal profit in the long run.

questions.enonce_markdown: What economic term explains the underlined phrase? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: **Price elasticity of demand.** Because there are many close substitutes, the demand for each firm's product is **relatively elastic** (elasticity greater than one, but not infinite): a small rise in price causes a fall in the quantity demanded that is proportionately larger, yet customers do not all leave, because brand loyalty built by product differentiation keeps some of them. In a perfect competitor's case demand would be perfectly elastic (infinite elasticity), and every customer would be lost.

questions.enonce_markdown: State one condition for a perfect competitive firm to operate at a loss in the short run. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: A perfectly competitive firm will keep producing at a loss in the short run when the **price is below average total cost but at least equal to average variable cost** ($AVC \le P < ATC$). At this price the revenue covers all the variable costs and gives a contribution towards the fixed costs, which have to be paid even if the firm closes down, so the loss is smaller than if it shut down. If the price falls below $AVC$, the firm should shut down.

questions.enonce_markdown: Enumerate any two ways in which a product can be differentiated. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any two of the following:

1. **Branding, packaging and design** (name, logo, colour, shape of the container).
2. **Quality, features or taste** (different ingredients, durability, performance).
3. **Advertising and image**, which creates brand loyalty.
4. **Location, opening hours and after-sales service** (convenience, delivery, guarantees).
